This substantial size is accompanied by a corresponding total wet body mass of approximately 390 grams [Wwi = approximately 390 grams] in fully grown adults, a value that places this freshwater clam among the larger members of the Mycetopodidae family. The attainment of such dimensions is a gradual process, underpinned by sustained filter-feeding activity on suspended organic matter throughout the animal's prolonged development. Field surveys of lentic and lotic habitats have consistently documented specimens approaching this upper size limit, although local environmental conditions such as water hardness and food availability introduce notable variation. The shell itself, typically thin but moderately inflated, provides a useful chronological record through growth checks visible on the external periostracum, allowing retrospective estimates of age and growth trajectory for individuals collected from different hydrological regimes.

This developmental milestone corresponds to a transition in energetic allocation, as gonadal tissue becomes macroscopically distinguishable from somatic mass. Juveniles below this size threshold remain reproductively quiescent, directing nearly all available resources toward somatic growth and shell accretion. The onset of puberty at 6.5 cm [Lp = 6.5 cm] represents a consistent pattern across multiple populations studied in South American drainages, though slight regional variation attributable to thermal regimes and trophic conditions has been documented. Once this length is achieved, individuals typically participate in the annual spawning cycle, with gametogenesis proceeding during periods of elevated water temperature and primary productivity. The relatively large size at maturity compared to other unionid and mycetopodid bivalves may reflect an evolutionary trade-off between delayed reproduction and the production of a more robust glochidial brood.

The life span of Anodontites trapesialis in stable warm-water environments has been estimated at approximately ten years [am = approximately ten years], based on mark-recapture studies and size-frequency distribution analyses conducted at a mean water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. The wet weight at birth for this species has been estimated at 0.000007 grams [Wwb = 0.000007 grams], a value derived from the dimensions of the glochidium larva which measures approximately 306 to 309 micrometres in length along its hinged axis. This minuscule starting mass underscores the extreme disparity between the newly released parasitic larva and the fully grown adult, which exceeds the birth weight by nearly eight orders of magnitude. The glochidium, upon release from the marsupial gills of the female, must attach to the gills or fins of a suitable fish host to complete its metamorphosis into a free-living juvenile. During this parasitic phase, the larva absorbs nutrients directly from the host's tissues, undergoing substantial morphological reorganization before excysting as a newly metamorphosed spat. Reproductive output in this freshwater clam is substantial, with gravid females releasing large numbers of glochidia during each spawning event. The fecundity per reproductive event has been quantified at several thousand larvae per brood, although the exact number is highly variable and depends on female size and somatic condition. Larger females approaching the ultimate shell length of 16 cm [Li = 16 cm] naturally produce proportionally more offspring, given the greater volume of marsupial gill tissue available for larval incubation. The production of such numerous, tiny glochidia with a wet weight at birth of only 0.000007 grams [Wwb = 0.000007 grams] represents a classic r-selected strategy within the brooding bivalve life history, offsetting high larval mortality during host searching and attachment. This high fecundity appears to be sustained over the species' decade-long life span of ten years [am = ten years] at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], ensuring that even modest annual recruitment can maintain stable population densities in habitats where fish hosts are reliably present. Understanding these reproductive parameters is crucial for conservation planning in impacted river systems.
